title: Readiness of Four Major Quantum Computing Platforms for Large-Scale Deployment
content: Quantum computing is an unconventional paradigm for executing numerical algorithms. It has progressed from theoretical principles to experimentally validated platforms, particularly: superconducting circuits, trapped ions, photonic systems, and neutral atom arrays. Quantum computing leverages principles of superposition, entanglement, and unitary evolution to enable computational and communication capabilities beyond classical systems. Our work serves as a brief topical review to examine the current state of quantum computing and the general readiness of quantum computing for large-scale deployment, including the requirements for fault-tolerant quantum error correction, hybrid systems, and modular architectures. Experimental benchmarking shows significant variation in coherence times, gate fidelities, noise profiles, and scalability constraints, with two-qubit gate errors emerging as the dominant limitation in the devices of the current era of NISQ (noisy intermediate-scale quantum). Our analysis shows that while significant progress has been made in the field of quantum computing, large-scale utilization seems to require coordinated advances in hardware engineering, error correction efficiency, materials science, and quantum networking. The presented outcomes highlight hybrid architectures as a promising pathway toward scalable and fault-tolerant quantum computing. Our study suggests that quantum computing is not hype, but it is in an early stage, and it may need more than two decades to become widely deployed. Even at its mature stage, quantum computers' utilization is expected to be focused on complex scientific simulations at large research organizations that can provide highly controlled physical environments, such as extreme cryogenic temperatures near zero absolute temperature.
